Level Measurement
Contact vs Non Contact Level Sensor: Which Is the Contact Type, How Each One Works and How to Choose

Some level sensors sit in the liquid and some look at it from above, and that single choice decides maintenance, accuracy and cost. We sort every common technology into the right group and show you how to pick one for your tank.

Float, DP, GWR Ultrasonic, Radar Comparison Table Level Calculator Selection Flowchart

Float, DP, capacitance and guided wave radar touch the process, while ultrasonic, radar, laser and nuclear gauges do not. We compare both groups and solve a time of flight example.

Hello everyone, today we are going to compare the contact vs non contact level sensor families, see which sensor is the contact type and learn how to select the right one.
Quick Answer

What is the difference in a contact vs non contact level sensor?

Contact vs non contact level sensor choice depends on whether the sensing part touches the process. Float, displacer, DP, capacitance, vibrating fork, magnetostrictive and guided wave radar are contact types, while ultrasonic, free space radar, laser and nuclear gauges measure from outside or above. For example, an ultrasonic sensor 5 m above the tank bottom with a 20 ms echo at 30 °C reads a level of 1.51 m.

PointContact typeNon contact type
ExamplesFloat, displacer, DP, capacitance, GWR, forkUltrasonic, radar, laser, nuclear
Touches processYes, probe, float or diaphragmNo, mounted above or outside
Coating and build upCan cause drift or stickingMostly unaffected
Vacuum, vapour, foamGWR handles foam and vapour wellUltrasonic fails in vacuum, radar copes
Typical costLow for switches and DPMedium to high, nuclear highest

What Is the Difference Between Contact and Non Contact Level Sensors?

In a contact vs non contact level sensor comparison, a contact sensor has a float, probe, rod or diaphragm that physically touches the liquid or solid, while a non contact sensor sends sound, microwaves, light or gamma rays from above or outside the vessel. Both give a level reading, but they differ in maintenance, process limits and price.

FeatureContact sensorsNon contact sensors
Working ideaBuoyancy, pressure, capacitance, guided pulseEcho time of sound or microwave, beam absorption
Wetted partsProbe, float, diaphragm, forkNone, only the antenna or face sees vapour
Best mediaClean liquids, interfaces, foam with GWRSticky, corrosive, sanitary or hot products
Weak spotsCoating, wear, moving partsFoam, dust, false echoes, blanking zone
InstallationLong probes, bottom nozzles, sometimes a liftSmall top nozzle, often 3 inch or less

Use the table as a first filter. For each technology in depth, see our article on types of level transmitters.

Do You Know?

The Wikipedia entry on level sensors lists radar transmitters working from about 1 GHz to 60 GHz, and it notes that non contact radar can even track molten metal above 1200 °C.

Which Is the Contact Type Level Sensor?

Any level sensor with a part that must sit in or touch the process is a contact type, and that includes float, displacer, DP or hydrostatic, capacitance, guided wave radar, vibrating fork, conductive and magnetostrictive sensors. They are simple and usually cheaper.

Float

A buoyant float rides on the surface and moves a reed switch or magnet.

Best for: Clean water tanks and alarms
Contact
Displacer

A displacer loses apparent weight as level rises, and a torque tube turns that into a signal.

Best for: Interface and boiler duty
Contact
DP or hydrostatic

A bottom pressure transmitter reads liquid head, so level is pressure divided by density and gravity.

Best for: Large tanks with stable density
Contact
Capacitance

A probe and the vessel wall form a capacitor that changes with the material around it.

Best for: Interfaces and small tanks
Contact
Guided wave radar

A microwave pulse travels down a rod or cable and reflects from the surface.

Best for: Foam, vapour and interfaces
Contact
Vibrating fork

A tuning fork changes frequency when the liquid covers it.

Best for: High and low alarms
Contact
Conductive

Probes complete a small current path through a conductive liquid.

Best for: Water and pump control
Contact
Magnetostrictive

A float magnet on a waveguide tube gives a precise time based position.

Best for: Custody and inventory tanks
Contact

Read our guides on the float level switch, the displacer transmitter and DP level measurement for wiring and calibration details. For probe based designs, start with capacitance level measurement and our guided wave radar transmitter article.

Guided wave radar confuses many students because it uses radar and still counts as a contact sensor. Its rod or cable sits in the liquid, and Wikipedia notes it shares the mechanical limits of an RF capacitance probe.

Quick Tip

If a sensor has a wetted part that you must clean or replace during a shutdown, treat it as a contact sensor in your maintenance plan.

What Are Non Contact Level Sensors?

Non contact level sensors measure from above or outside the vessel without touching the material, and the main types are ultrasonic, free space radar, laser and nuclear gamma gauges. They suit sticky, corrosive or hygienic products where a probe would coat or contaminate the batch.

Ultrasonic
Sends 20 kHz to 200 kHz sound pulses and times the echo, so it needs air or gas above the liquid.
Free space radar
Sends microwaves from a horn or lens antenna and is largely unaffected by vapour, pressure or vacuum.
Laser
Times a light pulse to the surface, useful for solids but blocked by dust and steam.
Nuclear gamma
A Cesium 137 or Cobalt 60 source and a detector sit outside the wall, so nothing enters the vessel.

For the details of each one, see our posts on ultrasonic level transmitter working, the radar type level transmitter and laser level transmitters. Nuclear gauges are explained in types of nuclear level measurement, and in India their sources fall under AERB licensing.

How Does a Non Contact Ultrasonic Sensor Calculate Level?

An ultrasonic sensor measures the round trip time of a sound pulse, halves it to get the distance to the surface, and subtracts that distance from the tank height to get level. Sound speed changes with air temperature, so good transmitters correct it with a built in temperature sensor.

Speed of sound: c = 331.3 + 0.606 × T m/s
Distance: d = c × t ÷ 2
Level: L = H minus d

Solved example: H = 5 m, t = 20 ms, T = 30 °C
c = 331.3 + 0.606 × 30 = 349.5 m/s
d = 349.5 × 0.020 ÷ 2 = 3.49 m
L = 5 minus 3.49 = 1.51 m

Skip the temperature correction and the error shows up quickly. If the same transmitter assumed 0 °C air, it would use 331.3 m/s, calculate 3.31 m distance and report 1.69 m, which is 0.18 m wrong on a 5 m tank.

The calculator below uses the same formula with the sensor height, echo time and air temperature.

Ultrasonic Time of Flight Level Calculator

Level 1.51 m (distance 3.49 m, sound speed 349.5 m/s)

Keep the level below the blanking zone, which Wikipedia puts at about 150 mm to 1 m depending on the transducer. You can cross check your result with the ultrasonic level calculator on Zenta during commissioning.

Contact vs Non Contact Level Sensor: Which One Should You Choose?

Choose a non contact sensor when the product would coat, corrode or contaminate a probe, and choose a contact sensor when you need low cost, interface measurement or reliable readings through heavy foam and vapour.

Non contact advantages
  • No wetted parts, so no coating, wear or corrosion of a probe
  • Small top nozzle, APG notes many fit a 3 inch NPT fitting or less
  • No contamination risk for food and pharma
  • Radar works through vapour, high pressure and vacuum
Non contact limitations
  • Foam absorbs ultrasonic pulses and can hide the radar echo
  • Ultrasonic cannot work in vacuum because it needs an atmosphere
  • Blanking zone and false echoes from nozzles and agitators
  • Higher price than a float switch or simple DP transmitter

Endress+Hauser explains that guided wave radar handles foam and condensation better than free space radar, while capacitance needs a metal vessel or a ground reference rod. Our comparison of non contact vs guided wave radar goes deeper into that particular choice.

Myth: Non contact sensors never need maintenance.
Fact: Condensation and build up on the antenna or transducer face still cause noise and false echoes, so faces need inspection.
Myth: Radar is always non contact.
Fact: Guided wave radar sends its pulse along a probe in the liquid, so it is a contact sensor.
Myth: Ultrasonic is as good as radar in any tank.
Fact: Ultrasonic is affected by temperature, vapour, dust and foam, and it fails completely in vacuum.

How to Select a Level Sensor for Your Process?

Start with the process conditions, then decide between contact and non contact, and only then compare range, accuracy and price.

1
Define the duty
Point alarm or continuous level, liquid or solid, and the required accuracy.
2
List the process limits
Temperature, pressure or vacuum, vapour, foam, turbulence and dielectric constant.
3
Check the media
Sticky, abrasive, corrosive or hygienic media point towards non contact.
4
Pick the technology
Use the decision path to shortlist two options.
5
Check the vessel
Nozzle size, obstructions and agitators.
6
Confirm cost
Compare price, spares and local service.

Our full guide on how to select the right level sensor adds solids, interfaces and safety duty, and the level switch vs level transmitter article helps you decide whether a simple alarm is enough.

Do You Know?

Endress+Hauser points out that radar reflection strength rises with the dielectric constant of the product, so oils and solvents return a weaker echo than water.

What Goes Wrong With Level Sensors in the Field?

Most level faults start in the process rather than the electronics: contact sensors suffer from coating and wear, and non contact sensors from foam, false echoes and condensation.

SymptomLikely sensor and causeFirst check
Float stuck at one valueFloat switch, sludge or crystal build upClean the float and stem, check the guide
Slow drift upwardCapacitance, coating on the probeClean the probe, recheck empty and full
Reading jumps to fullUltrasonic or radar, echo from a nozzle or ladderRun a false echo map with an empty tank
Signal lost when foamingUltrasonic, foam absorbs the pulseMove to guided wave radar or reduce foam
Wrong level after recipe changeDP, liquid density changedUpdate density in the transmitter range
Quick Tip

Before you blame the transmitter, open the echo curve or the live raw value. It often shows a false echo, a weak echo or a blanking zone problem that a setting can fix.

  • Mount ultrasonic and radar away from the fill stream and agitator blades
  • Keep the maximum level below the blanking zone of the sensor
  • Ground capacitance probes to the vessel or use a reference rod
  • Record liquid density for every DP level application
  • Run a false echo map on radar while the tank is nearly empty

For deeper fault finding, use our level transmitter troubleshooting guide and the article on radar false echo handling. Foam is covered separately in why foam affects level sensors, and slurry duty in level measurement in slurries.

Contact vs Non Contact Level Sensor FAQ

What is the main difference between contact and non contact level sensors?

A contact sensor has a float, probe or diaphragm in the process, while a non contact sensor measures from above or outside with sound, microwaves, light or gamma rays.

Float and DP are typical contact types, and ultrasonic and free space radar are typical non contact types.

Which level sensor is the contact type in a typical exam question?

Float, displacer, DP, capacitance, conductive, vibrating fork, magnetostrictive and guided wave radar are all contact type level sensors, because a part of each one touches the process.

If an option list shows ultrasonic, radar, laser and float, the float is the correct contact type answer every time.

Is guided wave radar a contact or non contact level sensor?

Guided wave radar is a contact sensor, because its microwave pulse travels along a rod or cable that sits in the liquid.

Endress+Hauser notes that it works at about 1.2 GHz and handles foam and condensation better than free space radar.

How to calculate level from ultrasonic echo time step by step?

First find sound speed as 331.3 plus 0.606 times air temperature, then distance equals speed times echo time divided by 2.

Level equals tank height minus distance, so 5 m with a 20 ms echo at 30 °C gives 1.51 m.

Why does an ultrasonic level sensor fail under vacuum or heavy foam?

Sound needs a gas to travel through, so there is no echo in vacuum, and foam absorbs the pulse before it returns.

In those tanks, free space radar handles vacuum while guided wave radar copes better with foam, according to Endress+Hauser.

Which level sensor is best for sticky, corrosive or food grade liquids?

A non contact radar is usually best, because nothing touches the product, so there is no coating, corrosion or hygiene risk.

APG also points out that non contact sensors avoid contaminating food and beverage batches, which a submerged probe can do.

Which is cheaper for a simple tank, contact vs non contact level sensor?

A contact float switch or a DP transmitter is normally cheaper than radar for a clean water or storage tank.

Non contact costs more upfront, but it can pay back on dirty duty where a probe would need frequent cleaning.

What We Learn Today

  • Float, displacer, DP, capacitance, conductive, vibrating fork, magnetostrictive and guided wave radar all touch the process, so they are contact type sensors.
  • Every contact vs non contact level sensor decision starts with process conditions such as coating, corrosion, vacuum, vapour and foam, before range or price.
  • Ultrasonic level equals tank height minus half the echo time multiplied by sound speed, and sound speed must be corrected for air temperature.
